# Background

In time-to-event analyses we often have to deal with censoring and competing risks, where for some subjects we only know that their event time was greater than a certain value.
For instance, we could be investigating whether a new drug prevents heart attacks in patients, but one subject moved overseas is no longer contactable, we only know they survived 
at least 6 months (censored). A different subject died at 1 years follow up from cancer (competing risk). For now let's ignore competing risks, and examine how to account for 
censoring when we want to calculate functions of the event time.

## Some notation

Let $T_i$ be the true event time and $C_i$ the censoring time for subject $i$. We observe:

$$\tilde{T}_i = \min(T_i, C_i), \qquad \varDelta_i = \mathbf{1}(T_i \leq C_i)$$

For a fixed horizon $\tau$ (e.g. maximum follow-up) the binary outcome of interest is:
$$Y_i = \mathbf{1}(T_i \leq \tau)$$

Let $\varphi(Y_i)$ be any function of the unobserved potential outcome $Y_i$. We want to estimate $E[\varphi(Y_i)]$ from observed data. For example, 
let $\hat{m}(t_i)$ be a predicted risk then the Brier score is defined by $\varphi(Y_i) = (Y_i - \hat{m})^2$. While a naive estimator for xxx is xxxx
this fails to xxxx and is systematically biased.

# Inverse probability of censoring weighting

The solution to censoring will be inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW). This method rebalances the data of the observed subjects to ensure ...... 
It does this by giving more weight to observations where it is likely their event time was censored rather than observed. This possibily depending on covariates.

## The core IPCW identity

Under independent censoring the following identity holds:

::: {.callout-note icon=false}

$$
E\!\left[\frac{\varDelta_i \cdot \mathbf{1}(t_i \leq \tau)}{G(t_i{-})}\,\varphi(Y_i)\right]
\;+\;
E\!\left[\frac{\mathbf{1}(t_i > \tau)}{G(\tau)}\,\varphi(Y_i)\right]
\;=\;
E\!\left[\varphi(Y_i)\right]
$$

where $G(s) = P(C > s)$ is the censoring survival function.
:::

This suggests the following sample analogue:

$$
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left\{
  \frac{\varDelta_i \cdot \mathbf{1}(t_i \leq \tau)}{\hat{G}(t_i{-})}\,\varphi(Y_i)
  \;+\;
  \frac{\mathbf{1}(t_i > \tau)}{\hat{G}(\tau)}\,\varphi(Y_i)
\right\}
$$

This looks reasonable straightforward to calculate; to get a censoring corrected estimate we just need to fit a model $G$ to the observed censoring times and balance the data using this model. 
Examples of such models would be Kaplan-Meier for plain $G(t)$ or a Cox regression model if we need to consider $G(t,X_t)$
There is nothing unusual here for anyone who has come across inverse probability of treatment weighting or related methods. 

But wait, why is it $t_i{-}$? Why not $t_i$? This is just because $G(s) = P(C > s)$, it has a strict inequality. We want to weight by the probability of censoring *at $t_i$ or after*, not 
just *after $t_i$* so we use $G(t_i{-}) = P(C > t_i{-})$.

## Proof

Much of the underlying theory for time-to-event data comes from stochastic processes, and in particular counting processes. While I have taken stochastic process courses I do not pretend 
to have deeply understood much. I've given my own intuitive understanding of the math where possible.

Probability...

Sample space, signma algebra, probability measure.

Jump times. Counting..

### Filtrations

Define the natural filtration $\mathcal{F}_t$ as the sigma-algebra generated by all information up to and including time $t$:

$$
\mathcal{F}_t = \sigma\!\left\{
  \mathbf{1}(T_i \leq s,\, \varDelta_i = 1),\;
  \mathbf{1}(C_i \leq s),\;
  s \leq t,\; i = 1,\ldots,n
\right\}
$$

A filtration $\mathcal{F}_t$ is just a way of making rigorous the idea of what information is available at a particular time. It is a 
mathematical model of the passage of time as the revelation of information. A jump time $\tilde{t}$ is just as noted above, a time when there is either censoring or an event. 

A process $H_t$ is **predictable** if it is $\mathcal{F}_{t-}$-measurable for all $t$, i.e. a probability can be assigned to it. 

Predictability means $H_t$ is determined by the past, strictly before time $t$.

### 3.2  The censoring martingale

Define:

- $N_t^C = \mathbf{1}(C_i \leq t,\, \varDelta_i = 0)$ — censoring counting process
- $Y_t = \mathbf{1}(t_i \geq t)$ — at-risk indicator
- $\lambda_t^C$ — censoring hazard

The censoring martingale is:

$$M_t^C \;=\; N_t^C \;-\; \int_0^t Y_s\,\lambda_s^C\,ds$$

By the optional stopping theorem, for any **predictable** process $H_t$:

$$E\!\left[\int_0^\infty H_t\,dM_t^C\right] = 0$$

This zero-expectation property is the engine of the IPCW identity.


### 3.4  Formal statement

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Theorem (IPCW unbiasedness)

Under independent censoring ($C \perp T \mid$ covariates), if $G(s) = P(C > s)$
is known, then for any bounded measurable $\varphi$:

$$
E\!\left[\frac{\varepsilon_i \cdot \mathbf{1}(t_i \leq \tau)}{G(t_i-)}\,\varphi(Y_i)\right]
\;=\;
E\!\left[\varphi(Y_i) \cdot \mathbf{1}(T_i \leq \tau)\right]
$$

**Proof sketch.** Write the LHS as an integral against the event measure $dN_t$.
The integrand $\varphi(Y)/G(t-)$ is predictable. Apply the optional stopping
theorem to the censoring martingale $M_t^C$. The compensator term recovers
$E[\varphi(Y_i) \cdot \mathbf{1}(T_i \leq \tau)]$ exactly. $\square$
:::
